1350.bp: When you type something into a search engine, the system has to figure out what you actually want. If you type 'best coffee', do you mean recipes, local shops, or product reviews? The real-world goal is simple: rewrite messy or unclear queries into crisp, focused ones that match what most people search for—this improves your chances of finding something useful.
1350.wh: Most systems today either ask a huge language model to rewrite your query (slow and expensive to run at scale), or they look at your personal search history (which doesn't exist for new users, and requires storing private data). The tricky part: what does the silent majority of people actually want? That signal gets lost. Smaller, lighter models can't capture what the mainstream search intent really is.
1350.ap: This system looks at millions of queries in real time and clusters together ones with the same intent—say, all the ways people ask about coffee shops near them. It finds the dominant themes in that cluster. Then it rewrites your query to match the mainstream pattern for that intent, without knowing anything about you personally. Separately, they train a smaller, lighter language model to mimic what a big powerful model would do—a transfer of skills from the expensive teacher to a cheap student.
1350.ww: When you align your query with what the population actually searches for, you're bypassing the need to know your personal history or pay for a huge model every time. The semantic clustering finds real intent patterns in the wilderness of search logs, and the lightweight model lets the system scale to millions of users in production without the cost and latency of a large model.
1350.po: In live tests on Baidu Search (millions of real users), this approach improved user satisfaction by 6.28% compared to existing methods. The lighter student model lets the company run this at scale in production right now, which is exactly what happened—it's been deployed in Baidu's live search system, handling real traffic.

1351.bp: Language models sometimes sound confident while saying things that are completely false—a problem called hallucination. If a model tells you a fact that matters (a medical diagnosis, a court ruling, a price quote), you need to know if it's actually true before you act on it. The real goal: catch these false statements before they reach a human.
1351.wh: When you ask multiple models the same question, they often agree with each other—but they can all be wrong together because they learned from the same data. If you assign one model to argue 'yes' and another to argue 'no', you're artificially forcing disagreement, and the fake disagreement might introduce new false claims. The hard part: how do you get different models to challenge each other genuinely?
1351.ap: Instead of assigning preset roles, the system generates a claim that directly contradicts the original statement (using formal logical rules as a safety check). It then asks independent agents to evaluate both the original claim and the contradictory claim separately, encouraging them to think through both sides. If they disagree, the debate happens naturally. If both sides agree (both true or both false), the agents explain their reasoning, and then they get to see what the other side said and update their view. A final judge reads all the arguments and makes the call.
1351.ww: When you debate a claim against its actual opposite—not a fake adversary—you force genuine reasoning about the substance. The logical safety check (Natural Language Inference) prevents the contradictory claim from being nonsense itself. Agents changing their minds after seeing opposing evidence is how you actually check if something is true or a hallucination—real reasoning beats stubborn agreement.
1351.po: The paper shows this works across question-answering benchmarks by catching false claims the models would have confidently repeated otherwise. The structured debate surfaces why a claim is false before it gets to a user who might believe it.

1352.bp: When a website shows you ads, they use a simple model: predict the probability you'll click it. But that prediction only matters if the numbers are trustworthy in the real chain. If the predicted click rate (pCTR) × the ad's bid price is used to rank which ads you see, then an ad that looks likely to get clicked might still fail if its predicted click rate is consistently off—you might get shown worse ads, or the auction math breaks down.
1352.wh: Most models obsess over a global metric called AUC, which asks: 'Can we rank items from most to least likely to be clicked?' But AUC is deaf to a sneaky problem: maybe the model thinks rare items (that almost nobody clicks on) will get clicked at 50% when they actually get clicked at 1%. The system looks good overall, but rare items have broken price signals. This is 'item-level calibration'—and it's been almost completely ignored because it's harder to measure and fix than just optimizing AUC.
1352.ap: The paper introduces a new metric to measure how wrong predictions are for each item category (group-wise absolute bias ratio), not just globally. Then they add a simple training trick: nudge the model during training to predict click rates that match reality for each item category, not just the population. The method is called TALENT and is a lightweight add-on to existing neural networks—you don't throw away the model architecture, just retrain it slightly differently.
1352.ww: When each item's predicted click rate is actually truthful, downstream systems that multiply pCTR × bid can make sane decisions. The ranking becomes fair to rare items because their low click rates are accurate, not pessimistically low. Better calibration means the whole auction and ranking pipeline can trust the numbers.
1352.po: Offline tests on real e-commerce platforms (Criteo, Avazu, KKBox) showed this improves both AUC and item-level calibration. More importantly, online A/B tests with millions of users showed measurable boosts in user response rates compared to methods that only optimized for AUC or calibration alone.

1353.bp: When you use an app like Facebook or Karrot (a local neighborhood app for buying/selling), the system learns what you like by showing you things and watching what you click. But the key insight is: not everything can be shown to you. On Karrot, you can only see items for sale in your neighborhood—that's a hard geographic boundary. The goal is to learn what you like without breaking this real-world constraint.
1353.wh: A standard trick in recommendation is to learn from 'in-batch negatives'—during training, the model is shown a user, an item they interacted with, and all the other items in the batch as 'negative' examples (things they didn't click). But this assumes any user could have been shown any item. On a geographically constrained platform, that's a lie: a user in Seoul will never see items for sale in Busan. The model learns that those Seoul-Busan pairs are negative, which is wrong—they're not negative, they're impossible. This noise dilutes the learning signal.
1353.ap: Instead of random batches, the system constructs batches where all users and all items are from the same region or nearby regions. This way, when the model treats other items in the batch as negatives, they're actually items the user could plausibly have seen. The negative examples become harder and more realistic, which teaches the model to learn better patterns.
1353.ww: When you only compare people against items they could actually encounter, the patterns you learn are trustworthy. If a user in Seoul likes K-pop merchandise, the model learns that from Seoul items they could see, not from a noisy mix of Seoul users paired with Busan items. The learned user pattern is cleaner and transfers better to ranking and retrieval tasks in real life.
1353.po: In live tests, region-constrained batching improved the quality of learned user patterns, which cascaded to better performance in home feed ranking, retrieval, and ad targeting. The deployed user embeddings are now in production across multiple applications on the platform.

1354.bp: When you're chatting with a doctor online about your symptoms, the conversation jumps around: you mention a rash, then ask if it's contagious, then ask what medicine to take. A good follow-up suggestion system anticipates what you might want to ask next, saving you time and helping you get better answers. The goal is to suggest the next sensible question based on where the conversation is right now.
1354.wh: The challenge is threefold: first, people clicking on suggested questions isn't a reliable signal of quality (some people click anything, others never click suggestions). Second, most systems separate retrieval (finding candidate questions) from ranking (scoring which is best). They optimize each step independently, so the ranked output might miss good questions that the retrieval step never considered. Third, each patient's medical state matters: if you said 'I have a fever', certain follow-ups make sense; if you're now asking about side effects, the context is totally different.
1354.ap: The system uses dialogue state tracking—a technique to extract and remember key medical facts from your conversation (symptoms, tests done, treatments mentioned). From this state, it retrieves candidate questions from two sources: a curated FAQ library and questions generated by a language model, both filtered using state-aware rules. A lightweight neural ranking model (a transformer) scores them, trained on real user preference data from past interactions. A feedback loop continuously collects what questions real users actually click and updates the ranking model.
1354.ww: Medical state is the connective tissue between retrieval and ranking: it lets you filter candidates intelligently at retrieval time and re-score them smartly at ranking time, so end-to-end performance improves. User preference data grounds the ranker in reality, not in guesses. The feedback loop adapts the model to what actually matters in your clinic.
1354.po: In live tests on a real online medical platform, this delivered striking gains: 23.5% more users clicked on suggestions, conversations lasted 59% longer (users asked more questions), and 19% more conversations were marked as successful by the patient or doctor.

1355.bp: Imagine a family shares one tablet and they all watch videos on it. The recommendation system learns from what everyone watches, but it's mixing patterns from multiple people. If the 8-year-old and the 40-year-old both watch on the same device, their preferences are tangled together, and recommendations become useless. The goal is to figure out who's actually holding the device right now, in real time, without waiting for enough watch history to untangle it.
1355.wh: Traditional solutions analyze watch sequences: if someone watches cartoons, then action movies, then cooking shows, the system guesses which part was which person. But this needs time—plenty of history to accumulate patterns. The hard part: you need to identify the person now, before they watch anything new. One subtle clue: how people hold and tap the device differs. A child swipes differently than an adult. But raw gestures are messy and entangled with video preferences during training—the model can't extract identity patterns cleanly.
1355.ap: The system clusters gesture patterns (how people hold and swipe) separately from the main recommendation model. Before feeding gestures into recommendations, it groups them via unsupervised clustering—finding natural gesture groups that likely correspond to different people. These cleaner gesture clusters become explicit identity signals that the recommendation model can use. It's like learning what makes each person's handwriting unique, then showing the handwriting to the model as a person-identity marker.
1355.ww: When you separate gesture clustering from the main recommendation training, the gestures themselves speak louder: they're not diluted by preference signals. The clusters capture how different people naturally move, and this becomes a fast, real-time cue of identity. Once you know who's using the device, personalization becomes meaningful for that person alone.
1355.po: The method worked on real short-video platforms handling multi-user devices, providing real-time identity cues that improved recommendations for each person. Gesture-based identification is instantaneous (no wait for behavior history) and performs better than methods that only use sequence patterns.

1356.bp: When you search for a flight on a travel website like Fliggy, you see a price listed. But by the time you click to book, the price might jump $50 because that cabin class sold out or the quoted fare expired. This breaks trust and kills the sale. The goal is to predict which flights will have price jumps and adjust ranking so users see flights that are likely to remain accurate.
1356.wh: Flight prices are volatile because seats are limited and get allocated in real time. A quote on the listing page might be stale by the time you book—it was cached to make the page load fast. Existing ranking models optimize for relevance and predicted clicks, ignoring this price volatility. Even if a flight looks perfect on paper, if its price will jump, the user's experience tanks. The tension: you can't predict with certainty which flights will have price jumps, and even if you could, you'd need to weight that uncertainty differently for different users.
1356.ap: The system has two parts. First, a pre-ranking module uses real-time inventory signals (which cabin classes are sold out) to guess which cached prices are stale and adjust them upward if needed—catching imminent price jumps before they shock the user. Second, a personalized attention mechanism learns each user's tolerance for price surprises (some people care a lot, others less). The ranking model adapts: for price-sensitive users, it boosts flights with stable prices; for flexible users, it weights price stability less.
1356.ww: Calibrating prices in real time reduces surprises, so users see flights that remain accurate. Learning how much each person cares about price certainty lets you personalize: you don't penalize stable-but-expensive flights the same way for everyone. Combining these makes the ranking honest and user-specific.
1356.po: Tests on Fliggy (a major travel platform) showed PCANet improved ranking accuracy and reduced price inconsistencies, which led to measurable gains in user engagement and booking completion rates—users were more willing to buy when prices stayed honest.

1357.bp: Flight search comes in two flavors: 'I want Beijing to Shanghai, July 5–10' (precise) and 'Show me cheap weekend trips from Beijing to anywhere' (fuzzy). Fuzzy search is exploratory—users don't know exactly what they want. These searches are common entry points but have very low conversion (only 1.6% of users who start a fuzzy search end up booking), because users are torn between many options and the recommendations feel generic.
1357.wh: Ranking models trained on precise searches don't understand fuzzy intent. In precise search, 'Beijing to Shanghai' is clear. In fuzzy, 'cheap weekend' is ambiguous and personal—two users with identical queries might want totally different trips. A model trained on precise queries sees 'destination: anywhere' and struggles; it's a domain mismatch. The offline metrics don't predict online performance because offline data is dominated by precise searches.
1357.ap: The system uses knowledge distillation: a large, powerful model trained on precise searches becomes a teacher. A lightweight student model learns to rank for fuzzy searches by mimicking the teacher's reasoning. The distillation has three parts: the student learns to produce internal representations (deep patterns) that match the teacher's; it learns to weight information by how confident the teacher is (uncertain knowledge is downweighted to avoid corrupting the student); and it learns to preserve the teacher's ranking order—if the teacher ranks trip A above trip B, the student does too.
1357.ww: The teacher trained on precise searches has learned subtle patterns about what makes a flight attractive (price, comfort, convenience). By transferring this knowledge to the fuzzy scenario, the student avoids the domain mismatch problem. Uncertainty-aware distillation prevents the teacher from misleading the student when its advice is shaky. Preserving ranking order ensures the student internalizes relative preferences.
1357.po: In tests, MCKD outperformed simpler distillation methods and baselines. Online A/B tests showed that offline gains translated to real conversion improvements in fuzzy flight search—more users who started exploring ended up booking.

1358.bp: When you type 'running shoes' into an e-commerce search, you're looking for shoes to buy, not ads for shoe brands. But the advertising system has to find relevant ads fast from tens of millions of products. The goal is to retrieve ads that match your intent and have high conversion odds, then rank them so the best ads appear first.
1358.wh: Speed and relevance are at odds. Traditional systems use a cascade: a fast retriever grabs candidates, then pre-rankers and rankers refine them, but each stage loses information and latency adds up. Because the system must respond in milliseconds, you can't retrieve enough candidates (only a tiny fraction of millions of ads even get considered). The pre-ranking stage doesn't have time to be smart, so ranking quality suffers. This is a classic tradeoff in recommendation: you have to pick speed or accuracy.
1358.ap: This system splits the work between offline and online. Offline (before the user even searches), for each query, it uses multiple retrieval methods (e.g., dense embeddings from BERT) to pull a large set of candidates. A language model designed for ads filtering removes irrelevant ones. A powerful neural ranking model scores the survivors. All this happens in the background, not during the live request. Online (when the user waits), the system fetches the pre-ranked results and applies only a final ranking stage using the most powerful models available.
1358.ww: By doing the heavy lifting offline, the online system is fast (single ranking stage, minimal latency). The offline language model filters out noise, so the ranker only scores high-quality candidates. More candidates are considered offline than ever fit through a live pipeline. The ranker gets better training data because it only sees relevant ads, not noise.
1358.po: This approach improved both retrieval quality and ranking accuracy compared to traditional online cascades. The e-commerce platform can show more relevant, higher-converting ads without asking users to wait longer.

1359.bp: Imagine a local marketplace app like DoorDash or Karrot: you want to buy coffee, and the app shows you vendors in your neighborhood. But vendors near you have fewer customers than popular vendors across the city, so recommendations often ignore them. The goal is to surface good but less-popular local shops without throwing away recommendations for the few popular ones everyone knows about.
1359.wh: Most recommendation systems learned from user interactions, and popular items get more interactions, so they dominate learning. The less popular items become 'long tail'—they're rare in training data, so the model's understanding of them is weak. Worse, in local-life services, items are inherently constrained by geography: a coffee shop in your neighborhood can only serve people nearby. This means each shop naturally has fewer interactions than city-wide shops. But that doesn't mean it's a bad shop—it's just local. Systems that optimize globally tend to forget that.
1359.ap: ReST starts by encoding what each item is (the shop's attributes: cuisine, hours, price range, location) into a representation. Then it uses a learning technique that contrasts each item against others, but with a twist: it only contrasts items that are spatially near each other. This encourages the model to learn what makes a local coffee shop distinctive compared to other local shops, not compared to the city's most famous café. The spatial constraint keeps the comparison fair.
1359.ww: When you only compare items with similar geographic reach, the model learns to appreciate local nuance. A quiet coffee shop in your neighborhood isn't penalized for not having a thousand interactions; it's compared fairly to other neighborhood shops. The attributes (cuisine, hours, etc.) also give the model semantic grounding beyond interaction counts, which helps for rare items.
1359.po: Tests on real local-life datasets and online A/B testing showed ReST surfaced long-tail items more effectively while maintaining performance on popular ones. The framework was plug-and-play, meaning it could be integrated into existing recommendation systems without rewriting everything.

1360.bp: When you contact customer support at a major e-commerce company like Flipkart, a human agent has to read your message, look up your order history, and craft a response. This is slow and repetitive—agents spend time retyping similar answers, and new agents take weeks to ramp up. The goal is to draft a response for the agent to review and edit, so they spend their time on judgment and exceptions, not boilerplate.
1360.wh: Drafting a good response requires three things: (1) knowing what you're asking (intent), (2) having the right context (your order, your history), and (3) following company policy (what the company is allowed to offer). A generic language model doesn't know your order details and might violate policy. A human agent spends too much time pulling this context together from multiple systems. The tension: you want AI to help, but not to make decisions or break rules—only to draft something for human approval.
1360.ap: AgentChat Copilot uses a pipeline: it first rewrites your latest message to include context from your chat history (so the system understands the full situation, not just your last question). It classifies your intent to know which order/account facts to retrieve. A retrieval module pulls relevant policy snippets and SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures). Finally, a generation model combines everything into a draft response in the company's tone. The human agent sees this draft, can edit it, and handles all the actual customer actions (refunds, replacements, etc.).
1360.ww: Splitting intent, context, and policy retrieval lets each component be simple and explainable. The human-in-the-loop design means the AI never makes commitments—it only proposes, and a human approves. This ensures brand consistency and policy compliance. The agent saves time on routine drafting so they can focus on tricky cases.
1360.po: Deployed at Flipkart, the system reduced Average Handling Time (how long each chat takes) by helping agents draft faster. It also improved consistency (less variation between agents) and reduced the onboarding burden for new agents. The system works across India's diverse customer base despite linguistic and cultural variation.

1361.bp: When a telecom company (like a cellular provider) wants to personalize an LLM's responses to you, they know a lot: what shows you watch, where you travel, who you call, which services you've complained about. The goal is to turn these behavioral signals into a coherent persona—a summary of what you care about—so an LLM can answer you more personally without leaking your private data.
1361.wh: The data is messy and sensitive: call summaries (transcripts), app usage logs, location patterns. You can't just paste all this raw data into a prompt (too much noise, privacy risk, cost). Smaller companies don't have resources to run massive LLMs on-premise, and cloud APIs aren't allowed (data must stay internal). The hard part: distilling diverse behavior signals into a structured persona that the LLM can actually use and understand.
1361.ap: PersonaPlugin processes 1M+ daily records entirely on the company's servers. It has specialized engines: the call extraction engine parses transcripts at >99% accuracy using cascading fallbacks (if one parser fails, try another). It then extracts structured facts: what you complained about, what services matter to you, where you spend time. These facts become a persona: short, structured sentences describing your preferences and concerns. When an LLM generates a response, the persona is injected as context.
1361.ww: Parsing and structuring behavior into personas is more robust than dumping raw signals into an LLM. The cascading parsers handle messy real-world transcripts (accents, noise, incomplete sentences). A structured persona is repeatable, auditable, and compact—the LLM can reason about it clearly. On-premise processing keeps sensitive data safe.
1361.po: Evaluation showed persona-based responses were significantly better: +24% improvement in personalization score, +26.7% in adherence to persona. Adding call context on top of behavioral personas yielded another +11% gain, showing the multi-source approach is synergistic. The system has been integrated into production.

1362.bp: Specialized domains (legal documents, medical literature, auditing records) have their own terminology and conventions. When you build a retrieval system for these domains, you need to rank documents by relevance within the domain's logic. The practical question: is it worth the time and cost to adapt a retriever to a specific domain, or will simple fine-tuning on a few examples work just as well?
1362.wh: The textbook answer is: collect lots of domain-specific training data and use domain-adaptive pretraining (train the model on domain language before fine-tuning). This is expensive and requires massive datasets. But in low-resource domains or languages, you might have only hundreds of examples. The tension: adaptive pretraining assumes you have tons of unlabeled data; fine-tuning on small labeled datasets is cheap but might underperform.
1362.ap: This paper empirically compares approaches: domain-adaptive pretraining using unlabeled and synthetic data, versus simple task-specific fine-tuning with just a few hundred labeled examples. They test across legal, biomedical, and auditing domains, plus two industrial Japanese datasets. They measure how much each approach improves over a general baseline.
1362.ww: When you have limited data, the extra signal from pretraining on domain language (learning 'legal-ese' or 'medical terminology') might not beat the focused learning from fine-tuning on the exact task you care about. Fine-tuning directly optimizes for relevance in your specific retrieval problem; pretraining is an indirect path. With synthetic data, even pretraining doesn't always win.
1362.po: The key finding: in the domains studied, task-specific fine-tuning with only a few hundred examples matched or beat domain-adaptive pretraining. On Japanese datasets, purely synthetic training data gave practical improvements. This suggests that for domain adaptation, companies should try the cheaper route (fine-tuning) first—domain-adaptive pretraining isn't always necessary and may not be worth the cost.

1363.bp: When you search for a laptop on an e-commerce site, you might start by saying 'under $1000', then narrow to 'gaming laptop', then switch to 'workstation' (realizing gaming isn't what you need). Each refinement is a constraint. The problem: the system has to decide which earlier constraints still apply. If you said 'I want under $1000' then switched to 'workstations', should the $1000 budget stick? Sometimes yes, sometimes no.
1363.wh: Existing systems use two extremes: 'persist all' keeps every constraint ever stated, which often leads to zero results (maybe no workstations exist under $1000). 'Clear all' starts fresh at each turn, so you re-explain yourself each time. Neither is satisfying. The hard part: automatically knowing when a constraint should survive a category switch is a reasoning problem that's domain-specific—only an LLM can really think through it.
1363.ap: CACS uses LLM reasoning to build a taxonomy of constraints: identity constraints (the item category itself, like 'laptop'), contextual constraints (current preferences, like 'gaming'), and session constraints (facts about you, like 'I have $1000 budget'). When you switch categories, a learned compatibility function decides which constraints transfer. Central to this is Constraint Persistence Reasoning (CPR)—the LLM reasons through a chain of thought: 'The user said under $1000 as a budget. Workstations also have prices. Workstations are more expensive than gaming laptops. So this constraint is relevant.' This reasoning is distilled into a lightweight classifier for production.
1363.ww: By classifying constraints into types and reasoning about relevance, the system avoids both over-persisting and over-clearing. The distilled lightweight model preserves the LLM's reasoning but runs fast. Users get sensible results (no zero-result dead ends) without re-explaining themselves constantly.
1363.po: Online A/B testing showed a 23% reduction in zero-result queries compared to existing approaches. Users had better experiences because the system was smarter about which constraints to carry forward, reducing the need to re-state preferences.

1364.bp: On enterprise platforms like Slack or Microsoft Teams, people search for past messages and files. But there's a problem: you can't ask users to rate relevance like Google does (too intrusive), and engagement signals like dwell time are noisy—if a message is long, you might spend time reading it even if it's not what you wanted. The goal is to get reliable training signals for what's truly relevant without asking humans or relying on clicks.
1364.wh: LLMs can read a query and a message and judge if it's relevant, giving you a semantic signal independent of user behavior. But LLM-only training produces models that ignore what users actually click on, degrading traditional search quality (users like it when things match their clicks). The tension: clicks are biased and noisy, but they capture user intent; LLM labels are semantically sound but ignore behavior. Neither alone works.
1364.ap: LLM-Click Agreement Labeling is simple: take only query-message pairs where an LLM judge and click-based labels agree that a message is relevant, or both agree it's irrelevant. Throw away the pairs where they disagree. This creates a cleaner training set: it includes pairs LLMs would call relevant that users also engaged with (strong signal) and pairs both say are irrelevant. It excludes LLM-only relevance (semantically right but users ignored it) and click-only relevance (users clicked but it might be a mistake).
1364.ww: By filtering to agreement, you keep the semantic rigor of LLM judgment and the behavioral grounding of clicks. You filter out noise from both sources—false positives from each. The resulting label set is smaller but higher-quality, so models trained on it learn a truer notion of relevance for the domain.
1364.po: In pilot testing with human annotators, agreement-based labels improved accuracy by +18% over click-only labels. In a large-scale A/B test across many users, this preserved traditional search quality while improving conversational features (users could cite and ground conversations better), with gains of +1.4% CiteDCG and +5.7% Good Citation Count. The lesson: supervision quality matters more than model architecture in large-scale retrieval systems.
